Updated assessment incorporating SLOOS signals:

- Credit supply conditions: SLOOS indicates broad easing of lending standards across residential real estate (including jumbo/QM and HELOC), CRE (multifamily and nonfarm nonresidential), and consumer credit (credit cards and autos). Banks also eased requirements, increased card credit limits, and reduced auto loan rates. This corroborates the FOMC’s view that overall financial conditions remain accommodative and supports growth and employment.
- Credit demand: Banks reported stronger demand for consumer loans and expect stronger demand for credit cards and C&I, while some categories showed mixed/softer spots (weaker current demand in autos and C&I; unchanged demand for construction and land development). Foreign banks reported stronger demand for CRE and mixed signals for C&I. Net, demand looks supportive, with pockets of softness tied to sector-specific factors.
- Risk appetite and vulnerabilities: Reasons cited for easing (economic outlook, competition, risk tolerance, liquidity/capital positions, secondary market conditions) suggest rising risk appetite, aligning with the FSR’s concern about elevated valuations and compressed risk premia. While tapering modestly tightens conditions, the SLOOS points to still-easy bank credit that could reinforce risk-taking.
- Net tone: Compared with the FSR-only lens (modestly positive but cautious), the SLOOS shows healthier credit intermediation and expected demand, nudging the tone slightly more positive, though vulnerabilities remain.
